reason: Both cited pages say what the claim asserts, at the scope asserted. The output-styles page's Proactive section states verbatim: "Claude starts implementing as soon as you send a task. It makes reasonable assumptions about routine decisions rather than stopping to ask... The style's instructions also tell Claude to check with you in the conversation before an action that deletes data or changes a shared or production system. That check is an instruction Claude follows and is separate from permission prompts... Switching to the Proactive style doesn't change your permission mode." This matches the claim's evidence almost word for word: immediate implementation, reasonable assumptions on routine decisions, a check-in before destructive/production actions, and no change to permission mode. The agent-sdk modifying-system-prompts page separately confirms the CLAUDE.md half of the claim: "Claude Code introduces your CLAUDE.md files with a line telling Claude that the instructions override default behavior" — the exact "introduced as overriding default behavior" framing the claim uses, and that page also lists "Output style instructions" as a separate, distinctly-introduced conversation reminder (not carrying that same override framing), which supports the claim's asymmetry point. I also checked the rule file directly: line 71 of llm-output.md contains the quoted text verbatim — "elsewhere, show the diff and wait for an explicit yes before generating a file" — so that quote is accurate too. Nothing in either page contradicts the claim or narrows its scope; the only unverifiable-by-documentation part is the claim's own interpretive conclusion (that the two "push opposite ways" and the override "is not declared as intentional"), which is reasoning built on accurately-cited facts, not a documentation-accuracy defect.

reason: The rule (line 85 of claude-code.md: "the harness reads any exit but the blocking one as no objection and lets a stalled pre-tool hook through on timeout") is about Claude Code's shell/command PreToolUse hooks (the kind the rule's own anchor names: `plugins/house/hooks/no-direct-master.sh`, tested via `tests/hooks/run.sh`), and the Claude Code hooks reference (code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks, Timeouts section) confirms it almost verbatim: "A timed-out command, http, or mcp_tool hook doesn't block the tool call. The call continues through the normal permission flow, so don't count on a stalled hook to act as a gate." The claim's contradicting quote — "Claude Code doesn't run the tool call... and the turn continues" — comes from a different section of the Agent SDK hooks page titled "Hook timeout," which is scoped to SDK-native callback functions passed via `options.hooks`, not to command/http/mcp_tool hooks; that same page (and the Claude Code hooks page's own PreToolUse note) explicitly carves this out: "An Agent SDK callback hook that exceeds its timeout blocks the tool call" — implying the default (command) hooks do not. So the claim conflates two distinct, separately-documented hook mechanisms and, at the scope the rule actually asserts (shell/command hooks), the cited docs support the rule rather than contradicting it; the claim's other listed evidence (deny rules evaluated regardless of hook return, settingSources gating project hooks/deny rules, parallel hooks with deny winning) is itself labeled "Consistent" by the claim and checks out against code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions, so nothing here actually conflicts with the rule.

reason: The docs frame CLAUDE.md and output styles as different, composable axes rather than opposed authorities: Proactive changes pace ('starts implementing... makes reasonable assumptions about routine decisions'... 'You can redirect it at any point') but explicitly 'doesn't change your permission mode,' is only 'an instruction Claude follows' that 'doesn't guarantee that something always happens or never happens,' and already carves out its own check-in exception 'before an action that deletes data or changes a shared or production system' -- i.e. Proactive itself treats 'routine' as bounded, not absolute. CLAUDE.md, by contrast, 'stays loaded whichever style you pick' and is introduced to Claude with 'a line telling Claude that the instructions override default behavior,' and the docs state the two 'combine' (CLAUDE.md for what Claude should know, output style for how it communicates). So the house rule's scoped procedural gate (explicit sign-off before generating output headed for the tracked tree or published surface, the llm-output module's own stated scope) is exactly the kind of project-specific narrowing of 'what counts as non-routine' that CLAUDE.md is designed to layer onto a style's baseline, not a command the style is built to override. Enforcement reality: the rule still adds real posture on top of Proactive -- it removes Claude's discretion over what counts as consequential for this scoped output class, discretion Proactive alone would otherwise leave to the model -- and nothing in the native feature covers or negates that; the apparent tension is already resolved by the documented priority (CLAUDE.md flagged as override, style self-limited to 'an instruction, not a guarantee'), so no rule-text change is needed to declare an intentional override.

reason: The CONFLICT rests on the Agent SDK hooks doc's PreToolUse-timeout behavior ("Claude Code doesn't run the tool call ... the turn continues," i.e. blocks), but that describes a different hook family: Agent SDK callback hooks registered programmatically via options.hooks inside a custom SDK application. The house rule and this repo's own hook (plugins/house/hooks/no-direct-master.sh, exercised by tests/hooks/run.sh) are a command/shell hook declared in settings.json, and the Claude Code CLI's own hooks doc explicitly calls out "the two hook families" on PreToolUse timeout, stating that for the command/http/mcp_tool family a timed-out hook "doesn't block the tool call. The call continues through the normal permission flow," which confirms rather than contradicts the rule's "lets a stalled pre-tool hook through on timeout" claim. The evidence's settingSources point is likewise scoped to Agent SDK-built apps, not the CLI's own bare/safe-mode/restricted-session hook loading that the rule's floor sentence is about. Because the cited native feature is scoped to a different surface (custom Agent SDK applications) than the one this rule enforces (Claude Code CLI settings.json hooks), it does not make the hook-fail-closed-and-test prescription redundant on that surface. The evidence's other observations (deny wins across parallel hooks, deny evaluated regardless of hook outcome) are real and are exactly the native floor the rule already cites to justify adding a managed-settings deny backstop, so the relationship is complementary, not conflicting.
